claims.text: Severe plastic deformation followed by controlled sub-recrystallization annealing can simultaneously improve strength and ductility in conventional metallic alloys.
The combined processing method can create a bimodal grain structure.
Conventional metallic alloys commonly exhibit a strength–ductility trade-off.
Severe plastic deformation refines the alloy microstructure.
Tailored sub-recrystallization annealing after severe plastic deformation can produce a gradient or bimodal grain-size distribution.
A bimodal microstructure contains ultrafine grains that impart strength and coarser grains that facilitate ductility.
Severe plastic deformation increases dislocation density.
Controlled annealing promotes selective grain growth after severe plastic deformation.
Ultrafine-grained regions provide high strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
Coarser-grained regions improve plasticity and ductility by accommodating more uniform plastic deformation.
The proposed processing route will increase yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure relative to conventional uniformly fine- or coarse-grained processing.
Conventional uniform grain refinement or phase-distribution strategies typically improve either strength or ductility, but not both concurrently.
Concurrent property improvement depends on achieving an optimized bimodal grain-size distribution.
Poorly controlled annealing or an overly uniform grain structure may prevent concurrent strength and ductility improvement.
